title.title: Nonnegative Ricci curvature can add harmonic functions
title.subtitle: Claim: metrics on $\mathbb R^3$ with $\mathrm{Ric} \ge 0$ carry more harmonic functions of growth $\le k$ than flat space

plain: Flat space has a fixed number of slow-growing 'balanced' functions; some gently curved spaces have more

beats.text: Flat $\mathbb R^3$ has $(k+1)^2$ harmonic functions of growth at most $k$
Yau asked whether $\mathrm{Ric} \ge 0$ can only lower that count (curves schematic)
The claim: for large $k$, a metric $g_k$ reaches $c\,(k+1)^2$ for any $c < 9v/4$

steps: Start flat near the centre, then let the metric oscillate far away
The space then looks different at every large scale
That leaves room for more slow-growing harmonic functions

achievement.label: Yau's harmonic dimension comparison
statement: h_k(\mathbb R^3, g_k) \ge c\,(k+1)^2 > (k+1)^2 = h_k(\mathbb R^3)
achievement.context: For every $v \in (4/9, 1)$, $c \in (1, 9v/4)$ and large $k$; $\mathrm{Ric} \ge 0$, Euclidean near 0
achievement.note: The metric depends on $k$: no single manifold fails for every $k$

verify.detail: Lean: an earlier 16-dimensional example with degree 50000, not the 3-dimensional theorem
verify.ourCheck: We read the Comparator statement; we did not build the Lean

voice.text: Flat space fixes the count of slow growing harmonic functions. Can curvature only lower it?
Keep it flat near the centre, oscillate far away, and extra harmonic functions appear.
Claimed: some curved metrics have more.

sources.quote: for every v in (4/9,1), c in (1, 9v/4) and all large integers k, a complete metric g_k on R^3 (Euclidean near 0, Ric >= 0, AVR = v) has h_k >= c (k+1)^2 > (k+1)^2
The metric depends on k (no single manifold violates it for all k).
